title: Naming a child
hook: a hukam is taken and the child named with the first letter of the hymn

segments.voice: Yesterday, the dastar: the turban that covers the uncut hair and that Sikhs call a crown. Your line was crowned. When did you act as if someone might remember it as yours? Day one thousand two hundred sixty-seven.

A new baby asleep in a car seat on the carpet of a gurdwara. Grandparents on one side, a nervous father on the other, the mother holding a bowl of karah prashad. Hymns of thanks are sung. Then the person attending the Granth opens it, not at a marked page but wherever it falls, and reads the hymn at the top of the left-hand page. Everyone leans in for one thing: the first letter. It's announced. Somebody whispers a name they've been hoping for, and it fits. Somebody else is already counting names on their fingers. That letter is where this child's name begins.
screen: `A BABY IN A CAR SEAT.` → `THE GRANTH OPENED WHERE IT FALLS.` → `EVERYONE WAITS FOR ONE LETTER.`

segments.voice: Naam karan means the naming. The Sikh Rehat Maryada describes it, in paraphrase, like this. When the mother and child are able, the family comes to the gurdwara with karah prashad. Hymns of joy and thanks are sung. A hukam is taken, the way we met last week: the Granth opened at random and the hymn at the top of the left-hand page read. The first letter of that hymn is announced, and a name beginning with it is chosen. Then the code adds the second name: Singh for a boy, Kaur for a girl. Ardas is said, and the prashad shared. Two things are worth holding. First, who chooses. The Granth gives a letter, not a name. People still choose, so the name is both a gift and a choice, the Guru's word and human love meeting on one letter. Second, the second name. The code gives a boy Singh and a girl Kaur, whatever family they're born into. Some readers see a quiet answer to caste in that: a surname can carry a caste, and Singh and Kaur carry none. Earlier this week, the code said no caste. Here, some would say, it's written into the name. This is the last day of the week, so look back. End well, at the bhog. Pray while cooking, with karah prashad. Explained, in katha. No lucky days. A tenth. Crowned. And now the name from the hukam, where a life's name begins in the Word.
screen: `NAAM KARAN: THE NAMING.` · `A HUKAM GIVES THE FIRST LETTER.` · `A NAME CHOSEN FROM THE LETTER.` · `SINGH OR KAUR FOR EVERY CHILD.` · then, large: `THE NAME FROM THE HUKAM.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: look up your name's meaning. Later today, if you don't know it, find out. For now, settle and breathe. Say your own name once, slowly, in your head. Think about who chose it and what they might have hoped when they did. If you know its meaning, hold that meaning for a few breaths. If you don't, hold the hope instead. Then let the name rest, the way a hymn rests after it's been read. The bell holds the time.
Naam karan. The Sikh naming: a hukam is taken, the first letter of the hymn is announced, a name is chosen from it, and Singh or Kaur is added. Today's word.

Your line: the name from the hukam. Today, learn the meaning of one name, yours or someone else's, and use that person's name with a little more care when you say it. Day one thousand two hundred sixty-seven.

notes: The naming steps are paraphrased from the Rehat Maryada (coming to the gurdwara when mother and child are able, karah prashad, hymns of joy, hukam, first letter, name chosen, Singh/Kaur added, Ardas).
